utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you begin, Mr. Milosevic, I'd like to mention two matters. Firstly dealing with the admission of exhibits, those tabs which were used during examination-in-chief which have already been used in examination-in-chief will be admitted, but thereafter, Mr. Milosevic, when you have used a tab, made reference to it, you should apply for its admission, if you wish, into evidence as an exhibit. This part of our proceedings is adversarial, and it is for the party to apply for the admission of a document into evidence. Secondly, at the beginning of the third session this morning, we'll have a brief discussion of Serbia and Montenegro's motion for the protection of diplomatic cables which will be used by the Prosecution -- or which may be used by the Prosecution in its cross-examination of this witness. I've set it for the beginning of the third session, Mr. Milosevic, because that would then coincide with the completion of the time that you had said would be spent in examination-in-chief. That's six hours. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the UN Security Council, with respect to the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- rather, the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina ever qualify those conflicts as some sort of foreign aggression or said that Serbia or the FRY was the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The UN Security Council didn't, nor did any other organ of the United Nations. The Security Council even -- what it did do in one Resolution in which it referred to the conduct of the three parties in Bosnia with respect to the peace plan of Vance and Owen pinpointed the three warring sides, two sides accepting the proposal and the third side that did not accept the proposal, and that third side was the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In point 47, and that's why I'm asking you about the Bosnian indictment, it says throughout the time to which the indictment refers in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was a state of international armed conflict and partial occupation. And since this speaks against me, if I can put it that way, it doesn't mean the partial occupation on the part of Croatian forces, which was quite obvious. Now, from the aspects of the FRY or Serbia, can this be considered correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. Not in any case, because Yugoslavia withdrew its last units, the units of the Yugoslav People's Army, which were composed of the citizens of Serbia and Montenegro. And on the other side, the -- on the other hand, the only foreign armed units that were in Bosnia were the units of the Republic of Croatia, and I remember that you in a conversation with the political director, Mr. Jacques Blot of the Quay d'Orsay, that you discussed this matter and indicated that factor, that his response to you was yes, we know all about that, we even know the numbers of brigades of the Croatian army in Bosnia, but the general perception is that you are to blame, and that's how things stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, take a look, Mr. Jovanovic, at tab 8.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, gentlemen, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this document is a report by the Secretary-General -- a report of the Secretary-General dated the 30th of May, 1992, and it is already in evidence as D91. I'm not sure that I understood you correctly, Mr. Robinson. Do I have to ask for that document to be admitted again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not if it has already been admitted. If it hasn't been admitted and you wish it to be admitted, then, yes, you must request its admission after you have used it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the topic in hand -- Mr. Jovanovic, have you found the report of the Secretary-General first?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to answer several questions pertaining to that report, and they are this: In paragraph 5, the General-Secretary says the following: "[In English] The bulk of the JNA personnel who were deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina were citizens of that republic and were not therefore covered by the Belgrade authorities' decision of 4 May to withdraw JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of them appear to have joined the army of the so-called 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina'. Others have joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is under the political control of the Presidency of that republic. Others may have joined various irregular forces operating there." [Interpretation] And then in paragraph 6 they say that according to the information of the Belgrade authorities, that is to say those who are not citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina which are covered by that decision, that they are barely 20 per cent of the total of that contingent, roughly, words to that effect. And then it says and the sentence begins: "Most of them are believed to have withdrawn [In English] already into Serbia or Montenegro, some of them having been subjected to attack during their withdrawal." [Interpretation] What do you know from that period of time about the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia with respect to what the General-Secretary -- Secretary-General says here and with respect to the attacks on the UN JNA units who were withdrawing from Bosnia and all the other matters mentioned in the report of the Secretary-General? And I'm going to draw your attention to a few of those later on.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Yugoslav People's Army or, rather, the JNA units were leaving en masse. They were made up of citizens of the republics that were breaking away from Yugoslavia, and that the same case was repeated in Bosnia when it came to the soldiers and officers who were there and who were not Serbs from that republic. So what happened was that the majority of members of the JNA in Bosnia were citizens of that republic, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they refused to carry on serving in the JNA and decided to stay on in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that was a general phenomenon that took place given the present circumstances and the break-up of Yugoslavia. Now, as far as the withdrawal of the JNA is concerned, I know that this was stated by the vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency. He made a statement to that effect. I think it was Mr. Kostic at the time, and he said that the JNA units had withdrawn from Bosnia and that what remained were just several smaller pockets. I think there were some cadets that he referred to in Sarajevo, several hundred cadets in Sarajevo and elsewhere, and their withdrawal was systematically prevented by part of the leadership of the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So those men who did not withdraw were in fact blocked in those pockets, the few pockets, by the Muslim militia or police or, rather, the so-called Territorial Defence, the Muslim Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely it. And their goal was, I assume, to seize the weapons these men had and to provoke them in order to be able to proclaim the JNA as the aggressor in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, what is the source, your source for that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source of this information is not only this report, and you can see it right through the report, as well as a series of other reports which were compiled by the United Nations representatives. For example, General MacKenzie in his report or, rather, in his memoirs spoke about certain of these facts, and I have the impression that something similar was said by another British general. What was his name? Michael Rose, I believe. So that you can read that up there in several reports and also the reports by foreign correspondents dating back to that period indicate that, indicate that matters evolved along that course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Those are foreign sources. But what about your own? Do you have personal knowledge from that period of time about the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from Bosnia-Herzegovina, for example?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because those statements were made by the top leadership, the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army at the time, and this was confirmed and borne out by the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia itself. And in public statements and in the press the difficulties were highlighted that certain units were encountering during their withdrawal from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and even that there were some bloody conflicts in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the vice-president of the Yugoslav Presidency at the time, Mr. Branko Kostic, had a meeting with the then president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, and proposed that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, since that was after the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, should take steps in order to take what was theirs from the JNA on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that, and I do know that Mr. Izetbegovic, afterwards, did not agree to attend another meeting to decide the specifics of that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no other way out, nothing else to do but for the JNA, by order of the Yugoslav state Presidency, to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was done, and that is reflected in this report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last two questions have both been really effectively leading questions. The witness is speaking unclear as to the source of his knowledge and information, and I don't have any document or 65 ter summary to explain to me where it all comes from. So I'd invite the Chamber to restrain these leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've again been asking leading questions. The Chamber has been fairly flexible with you, but I'm quite satisfied that you can ask questions that are not leading, and the Chamber expects you to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I hope I'm not going to ask leading questions, but bear in mind that this is not a witness that learnt something from reading the papers. He was the former foreign minister, so he had access to all kinds of information during the material period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's all the more reason why you should avoid asking leading questions. He has the information. Let him present it. And I think you have the technique.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to say that if his answers are going to be based on documents, then either he must produce them, or at the very least he must identify them so that we can see if we have them; alternatively, that we may be able to find them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it all goes to weight and the value that will be attached to his evidence. Mr. Milosevic, the rule against leading questions is particularly relevant in areas of controversy, in matters of dispute. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I'd like to draw your attention to -- I'd like to draw your attention to the middle of paragraph 9, one sentence there which states the following: "[In English]... it is also clear that the emergence of General Mladic and the forces under his command as independent actor -- independent actors apparently beyond the control of JNA greatly complicates the issues raised in paragraph 4 of Security Council Resolution 752." [Interpretation] Then it says: "[In English] President Izetbegovic has recently indicated to senior UNPROFOR officers at Sarajevo his willingness to deal with General Mladic but not with the political leadership of the 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.'" [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention to what it says here. "[In English] ... forces under his command as independent actors apparently beyond the control of JNA." [Interpretation] Do you know -- do you know -- I'm trying not to lead you. Do you know under whose control the forces of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina it was known at the time, later Republika Srpska, were?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any direct knowledge about this, but my impression was at the time that at least at that time the forces of Republika Srpska were still in the making, and they were fully independent. They behaved as such in the field as well. So that period of the establishment of the forces of Republika Srpska was practically a period of their absolute independence from any kind of external influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you say "at that time," do you know perhaps anything about a later time; namely, that the army of Republika Srpska was under some kind of outside control, under the control of someone outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, outside Republika Srpska? Do you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information to that effect that it was under anyone's control, because quite simply I was not in contact with their top military people. But my impression is from various discussions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That simply goes to show the reality of the previous answer, or to be precise the complete lack of reality of the previous answer. We hear something that is the witness's impression. He's asked a question, Do you know under whose control the forces of the Serb republic were? He says, My impression is this, then he gives knowledge of something that is negative, and then he goes back to another impression. Are impressions of any value to this Chamber? I would invite the Chamber to say that without clear exposition of what the impression is based on, the answer must be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just raise some matters here? This is a witness who was present at the time, involved essentially in many of these important issues. He may not have been in place so that he was aware directly and through his own contact with what was going on, but he was in a part of the events that he was aware that things were happening elsewhere because of his positioning and place, and for him to give his impression from where he was is important evidence that the Trial Chamber can attach what weight it feels fit to eventually, but bearing in mind where he was. I was reading the transcript of Mr. Nice's questioning of Mr. Bakalli yesterday, and exactly the same objection he is making now could be levelled directly at him on page 516 of the transcript. The impressions of Mr. Bakalli concerning tanks outside the Assembly building in Pristina, the impressions of Mr. Bakalli about Gazimestan. All these issues were ways that Mr. Nice built his case, but we have here exactly the same kind of witness for the Defence who had a role to play and is able to give information of what he was aware was happening elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Milosevic, in my view -- in my view, the passage that you have cited from the Secretary-General's report is very, very important to your case. It's very, very strong evidence. Although it says that the forces under his command, that is General Mladic, were apparently beyond the control of the JNA, the word "apparently," of course, is significant, but I would suggest that you try to get a witness other than this witness who can substantiate what the Secretary-General says in his report. Even without that substantiation, as a report from the Secretary-General, I would attach great weight to it, but I think your case would be immensely strengthened if, for example, you could secure the authors of the report. I mean, you very well know that it is not the Secretary-General himself who wrote it, but the person in the UN who would have received specific information on this issue and who would have compiled the report might be able to give valuable evidence in relation to your case. But I don't think this witness can take it much further beyond his impressions, and we can't rule that evidence out, but the weight that we will be able to attach to it is a matter that we'll have to determine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, in relation to that, may I add just one sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, briefly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that on the occasion of later attacks of the army of Republika Srpska at some targets in Bosnia-Herzegovina, President Milosevic was very surprised and very bitter. For example, the mountain of Igman and Bjelasnica near Sarajevo in 1993, then the shelling of Gorazde in 1993, then the attack on Srebrenica in 1993. He was embittered when he learned that that happened, and he was outraged that it happened. That, in my opinion, is proof that the forces of Republika Srpska were not under his control. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, please. When I put a question to you, could you tell me what your actual knowledge is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you yourself said that Mr. Jovanovic is obviously a career diplomat. You learned that from his CV. So his language is rather diplomatic. So what other people would say that they know of, Mr. Jovanovic says it is his impression. It is simply the way he speaks. But it is a fact that he knew about, so there is no denying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's for him to clarify whether it's his impression or whether he's speaking from actual knowledge, Mr. Milosevic, it's not for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a degree of understanding for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But, please, Mr. Jovanovic, would you clarify.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about Article 9 -- we are talking about Article 9, are we -- or, rather, paragraph 9. It is quite clear that the forces of the army of Republika Srpska and General Mladic were not under the control of the JNA or Serbia at that time at all, because everything that happened there was news from the outside that were coming to Serbia and to its leadership as something that is new and something that we were not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In order to clarify this a bit more, could you please look one paragraph up, that is to say paragraph 8, where it says: "[In English] A senior JNA representative from Belgrade, General Nedeljko Boskovic, has conducted discussions with the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency, but it has become clear that his word is not binding on the commander of the army of the 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina,' General Mladic." [Interpretation] I think that there is yet another element there which leads to a particular conclusion. What is the conclusion that you draw on this basis or, rather, what did you know at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that General Mladic was defiant, and he was challenging General Boskovic. He didn't want to cooperate with him, and he didn't want to take his advice. So he acted in total independence, without taking into consideration what the JNA representatives were telling him or advising him to do. This report reflects that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at paragraph 10 now. "[In English] As regards the withdrawal of elements of the Croatian army now in Bosnia-Herzegovina ..." [Interpretation] Is this a statement that there are elements of the Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina now? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Yes. As I said a few minutes ago, what Mr. Blot told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then the sentence continues: "[In English] ... information currently available in New York suggests that no such withdrawal has occurred. UNPROFOR has received reliable reports of Croatian army personnel, in uniforms, operating within, and as part of, military formations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian authorities have consistently taken the position that the Croatian soldiers in Bosnia and Herzegovina have left the Croatian army and are not subject to its authority. International observers do not, however, doubt that portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina are under the control of Croatian military units, whether belonging to the local Territorial Defence, to paramilitary groups, or to the Croatian army. It is unclear in the circumstances how their withdrawal or disbandment, as required by the Council, can be achieved." [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, isn't this report clear? Does it not clearly show a contrast between the information in the report of the Secretary-General about the attitude of the JNA towards this matter and the attitude of the Croatian army? What kind of information is provided about one and what kind of information is provided by the other?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is obvious. The presence and withdrawal of the JNA are referred to in a positive sense as a process which is practically completed except for a few pockets which made it impossible for them to withdraw completely, whereas the presence of Croatian regular forces - I mean the Republic of Croatia - is spoken of in a very unequivocal manner. Some soldiers of the army of the Republic of Croatia voluntarily joined their brothers in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but then there were also regular forces there of the Croatian army with the presence of certain brigades by numbers, Mr. Blot said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about this report of the Secretary-General? It was supposed to be debated before a decision was passed on imposing sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This report came with a delay. The members of the Security Council, had they received it on time and read it on time, I'm sure that they would not have voted in favour of the Resolution for imposing sanctions against Yugoslavia. There would not have been any factual basis, or any legal basis or political basis for it. However, it came with a delay. According to what we learned later, this was no accident, this delay. Allegedly, it was done by an administrative officer who was allegedly instructed to drag his feet on this. So this was a manipulation, to the best of our knowledge, of the Security Council in order to have a particular decision pushed through. The Security Council certainly would not have passed such a Resolution had it known about this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Obviously if we can have the name of the administrative officer or matters of that sort, we can put matters, start inquiries straight away, but without particulars it's all a bit vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it really matter, Mr. Nice? Is that really the point of this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it matters or not, but we find ourselves recurringly in the position of having these very broad, sometimes very serious, allegations made, and I hope to be able to leave cross-examination, which I hope to be brief, having identified issues where they should properly be identified. Now, to say that the -- the Secretariat of the United Nations hasn't been free of criticism thus far. There's been criticism indeed coming from a witness called by me. But nevertheless, if allegations of this kind, really rather serious allegations are going to be made, it is better that we should have the detail, if it's available, straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But as Judge Bonomy said, nothing might turn on it, because the report is nonetheless there and it does contain, in my view, information which is quite helpful to the case of the accused. The fact that it wasn't presented to the Security Council or that it may have been, by some alleged manipulation, kept from the Security Council is really neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the problem there, Your Honour, is I think the accused will rely on the alleged manipulation, but I've probably taken enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He may rely on the fact that it didn't go to the Security Council. I understand that. But why it didn't go doesn't really seem, for the purposes of this trial, to be terribly important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The point is that we have the report. Mr. Milosevic, it has occurred to me that hopefully we're not far away from the -- too far away from the close of your case, and I just wonder how you're managing your case. For example, when you come to make your closing submissions, I think you need help. You will need technical help to isolate matters of importance to your case and to highlight them, like, for example, this report. And you should really be utilising the services of the assigned counsel. I mean, you may want to use your closing address for other purposes, but there is a lot of material in the case which could be helpful to your case and beneficial for your case, and it would be a pity if you are not utilising your closing address in a meaningful way. And you have a wealth of material before you. There's just so much information, so much material in this case, and it is my view and I think the view of the Chamber that you should be utilising the services of the assigned counsel to assist you in matters of that kind. But I just make that observation. Continue with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, let me just clarify something, what you said in relation to the report. This report did reach the Security Council. The point is that it did not arrive on time. It was one day late. But this report did reach the Security Council, and the Security Council did debate it, did have a look at it. It's not that it did not reach it at all, it was just delayed through this manipulation. But it is a document that was looked at by the Security Council. But let me proceed, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, now let us move into the political arena which is very familiar to you. Why is it that Serbia or, rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia supported the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what were the real goals of that support that was provided?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia supported its own people in Bosnia and Herzegovina just as any other state would do in relation to its people in similar situation, because the Serb people were denied their constituent rights by the referendum that was organised and through the decisions of Badinter's commission and later the decisions of EU which turned that nation into a minority. Therefore, its constituent rights, its safety, its normal, regular life were endangered. That's why Serbia supported its people, its right to self-determination, to equality, and to freedom. Once that was achieved, and that was done through Cutileiro's plan on the 17th of March, 1992, Serbia supported that. Serbia supported the idea of independent Bosnia and Herzegovina organised on the basis of cantons. This is another fact showing that Serbia did not support Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a result of its territorial ambitions but, rather, because their existential rights, their rights to freedom were jeopardised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the course of the conflict, you took part in many meetings. You had numerous contacts that we had at the time with international mediators and so on. What do you know about the demilitarisation of the airport in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this problem came about rather early because the airport was quite important for the functioning of the town and for the functioning of UNPROFOR. Therefore, the request to demilitarise the airport, which was put in by the international community, is something that you and other organs from the SFRY supported and supported continuously from the very beginning. In that sense, you used your political influence over the political leadership of Republika Srpska to urge them to accept that request. You did that in all of your contacts with international mediators and other interlocutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was the airport finally demilitarised and was it taken over by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That did come about after a certain delay, and from that time on the airport was in use except when there were -- there were combat activities in the vicinity of the airport and the airport had to be closed because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was our position with respect to the shelling of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. From the very beginning, at all levels we, the Presidency of SFRY, the government of the republic, you personally and I, in numerous statements condemned the shelling and demanded that the authorities of Republika Srpska cease that activity. You did that publicly and also in all of the discussions you had with representatives of international community mediators and everybody else who came to see you and talk to you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You were present when the discussions with Douglas Hurd took place in Belgrade in July of 1992. I think that it was on the 18th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that conversation?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of conversations or meetings covering same topics. However, I remember that even at that time the issue of the shelling of Sarajevo was raised and that on that occasion you yet again presented your attitude to Mr. Hurd, namely, saying that you were opposed to it and that you condemned that kind of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our views, positions were quite public. It's not that they were expressed just in the conversation with Mr. Hurd. Was the London conference in progress then?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was held in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So just a month later.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that before that representatives of warring sides concluded a cease-fire agreement, if I remember well. You supported that agreement, and reiterated that in your contacts with Mr. Hurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Jovanovic, how did the news about some camps reach us, and how did we react to those news?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received those news through the foreign media, and we were very critical with respect to that. However, later on when we asked that that be verified and when we approached the authorities of Republika Srpska, we received an answer that those were not concentration camps but, rather, collection points, holding centres for the soldiers of the opposing side, and that they were of a temporary nature. We asked that those facilities be disbanded even though they were not concentration camps as we were assured and as the foreign media claimed. Naturally, there were some abuses in certain parts, but it's also quite natural that the political leadership of Republika Srpska could not have known about everything that was going on in the entire territory of the entire country in view of the fact that there was war going on, that communications were disrupted, the corridors were blocked, the corridors that would enable them to have contact with that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina where it was said the camps existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In order not to use diplomatic language, Mr. Jovanovic, did I understand you well, namely, did you say that based on what we received, the information that we received, it seemed that the leadership of Republika Srpska didn't know about those facilities? At least, that's what they told us. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we asked them whether it was true what the foreign media reported about, they denied it. They said it wasn't true, that those were not camps but, rather, collection points, collection centres. And based on that, we had an impression that they themselves knew nothing about the existence of such sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to refer now to previous times and to Kosovo, but please tell us, do you know about the term "ethnic cleansing," and do you know what we in Serbia, what I personally, our leadership in Serbia believed about the persecution of population that was driven by racial or ethnic considerations and so on?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "ethnic cleansing" was first used in the 1980s, in early 1980s, during the demonstrations organised by Kosovo Albanians when they used slogans "Kosovo Republic" and "Kosovo for Albanians only." We at the time publicly condemned any activity that would resemble ethnic cleansing or anything similar. You stated that publicly yourself. For example, after the conference in London, you declared that you strongly condemned any activity, any kind of ethnic cleansing, any forcible moving out of population from one place to another. And you said that if there was any such activity going on, it needed to be halted immediately. And this is something that was frequently repeated at all levels by representatives of the Serbian government, federal government; you yourself stated this on numerous occasions, as did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I say that should it be established that such activity was committed by somebody, those people needed to face justice?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You said that if there was ever a crime that could never be condoned or accepted, if such crimes were committed at any point of time, then those people needed to be held accountable for that. You stated that publicly on many occasions, including immediately after the London conference at a press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were present when we met with Carter in December of 1994.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what were the main points? Do you remember anything particular from that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he said that during his previous meeting with Mr. Karadzic there were a number of points discussed, perhaps six points, and that you supported all peace efforts, including the peace initiative of President Carter. However, you pointed out that you had very poor contacts and communication with the leadership of Republika Srpska and that you could not influence their position much. Mr. Carter applauded your position, and he stated that he was expecting his mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina to bear fruit. Unfortunately, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, in 1994 and in 1995, we had poor communication or, rather, we were on rather bad terms with Republika Srpska. Do you remember, why was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was due to, first of all, their refusal to accept Vance-Owen Plan and then Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. And as a result of that, our Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relations were strained. Occasionally we had no contact whatsoever with them. So there was no cooperation, state cooperation or any other cooperation. Our meetings were mostly devoted to the disputes and disagreements we had rather than any kind of cooperation. These strained relations escalated at the time when the Contact Group plan was circulated and when the leadership of Republika Srpska consistently refused, for various reasons, some convincing, some not, to accept that plan. This led to increasing difficulties in our relations, even to disruption of any communication. And finally, the decision of government of Republika Srpska was adopted on the 4th of August, 1994, I believe, to halt all contacts with the leadership of Republika Srpska and also all economic contacts, to ban their leadership from residing in Serbia. Only food, clothing, and medication was exempted from this embargo. This is what the situation was up until the beginning of the Dayton negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't think that we would turn to this, so my recollections are not that fresh, but did you attend that fateful meeting where the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church was present as well and when finally an agreement was reached to establish one single delegation for negotiations in Dayton?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present. I was in New York at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then we will not put any further questions about that. Do you remember the hostage crisis and the reactions of Serbia and myself personally to that crisis?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly remember. This involved 282 hostages, members of UNPROFOR, which were taken hostage by the forces of Republika Srpska in order, as they alleged, to protect themselves from the bombing by NATO aviation. When we heard about that, we were shocked. We were surprised. We condemned that action, and through contacts with the international community and the leadership of Republika Srpska, we did our best to ensure safety for the hostages. But despite strained relations with the leadership of Republika Srpska, we managed to give a major contribution towards releasing hostages and ensuring their safe return to their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, do you remember Stoltenberg's visit to Belgrade in late July 1995? I have a note here that it took place on the 29th of July, 1995. Stoltenberg came to visit, and as far as I can see here, you attended that meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that I did, although there were numerous meetings with Mr. Stoltenberg, and I'm sure that I was present if I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that discussion with Mr. Stoltenberg?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember it precisely because a lot of these discussions were very similar, resolving around similar topics. It had to do with the Contact Group plan, and I can't remember whether we discussed anything else. Can you remind me about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in order to avoid putting leading questions, let me just tell you that at the time, attempting to ensure that the plan is accepted, we tried to recruit some members of the parliament of Republika Srpska to support the plan. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You informed Mr. Stoltenberg and then other representatives who came later about that. You worked tirelessly on ensuring that there was an increased number of the members of parliament of Republika Srpska who would support the plan and vote in favour of it. And you did that through various channels, various intermediaries, and I think you told us that that number increased to 36 or 38 MPs who were already ready to vote in favour of that proposal, and I think that the total number of MPs were 70 or 78 in their parliament. And when asked when you expected this number to reach an absolute majority, you stated that you expected that very soon. I think that Dr. Owen put that question to you. Unfortunately, that didn't happen. But at the time, you were convinced that this number would be able to reach a number over 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The number was supposed to exceed 50, but afterwards, the chance fell through. Let me just have a look at my notes here. Do you remember when a whole brigade of the Muslim army, after I gave approval, crossed the Drina River to save themselves from the offensive and the fighting that was going on at the time in Eastern Bosnia? Or, rather, this is a fact, there is no need for you to confirm it, but do you remember the letter I addressed to Alija Izetbegovic on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember the crossing of that unit, and I think it was deployed at Mount Tara or Mount Zlatibor until they were taken over by the International Red Cross. And I remember that you sent a letter to Alija Izetbegovic and a letter with similar contents was also sent to Ratko Mladic, asking both these two men, in the interests of peace, to put a stop to all the fighting immediately. And you also said that there was no justification for increasing the number of victims and killing people when we already had a plan in place which would lead to a peaceful political and democratic settlement to the crisis. And you informed Mr. Izetbegovic that you had sent a similar letter to General Mladic with similar contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the visit by Malcolm Rivkin? You were present, I believe.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have anything that you remember that would be characteristic from that visit?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he gave recognition to you personally for everything that you had done and were doing for the Contact Group's plan, to further the plan. And I know that later on, when the Dayton agreement was signed, he also made a public statement in which he emphasised your great contribution to the entire peace process and especially the Dayton agreement coming about through your good offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how intensive -- or, rather, it doesn't matter if you remember - I'm sure you do - but do you recall our intensive cooperation with the special UN Secretary-General representative for Yugoslavia, Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember he was a very frequent visitor to Belgrade and that we always had concrete, constructive talks on matters that he raised, and he raised a number of issues, and he was different from the international mediators, Stoltenberg and Owen. These questions were relatively lesser questions relating to various incidents, so they were of a lesser order. But he always appealed to Vance for support and efforts to overcome the problems. He appealed to you to overcome the problems, and you did help, and he said that at the end of his mission during a press conference in assessing his cooperation with you throughout his sojourn in Yugoslavia. And he dealt with Bihac, for example, Republika Srpska Krajina, the shelling of Gorazde, and so on and so forth, many of these incidents that took place on a daily basis as the war developed and as the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina developed. And I think it was -- he was extremely grateful to you, at least that's what he said, for all the assistance you had given to help solve those issues. And sometimes during those conversations Mr. Martic would be present, especially towards the end when the situation around Bihac developed, and you answered in front of him that all matters, all issues must be resolved by peaceful political means and not by force of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned Mr. Martic just now, do you remember that at that time we had a very positive process going on to regulate relations between Knin and Zagreb, for instance, and what our attitude towards that process was, the process of mutually regulating relations between Knin and Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a process which incorporated regulated cooperation or, rather, having the basic life system restored between Knin and Zagreb, which means the gas pipeline, the water pipeline, and all other means of cooperation between Croatia and the Republic of Srpska Krajina. And I don't know where the agreement was actually signed, whether it was in Knin or Erdut, but I do know that this question was often on the agenda of your meetings, both with the representatives of Republika Srpska Krajina and with the representatives of Serb Croatia as well and of course with international representatives, too, and that you always insisted upon very detailed and expedient undertaking of responsibilities that were taken on on the basis of your agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, do you know that in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina which went on, you know that there were large numbers of refugees, but do you know how many Muslim refugees fled to Serbia, fled from the conflict that was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina and fled to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were between 50 and 70.000 of them and that they fled during the war operations and when there weren't, when they expected another onslaught. I personally met some Muslims who worked in the Belgrade Circus and other places who talked to me about that and said that they wanted to get out fast in order to avoid the war conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The treatment of these refugees was equal to the treatment of Serb refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and indeed from Croatia as well. Everybody was treated equally. We had a total of 700 or 800.000 from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. The largest number were, of course, Serbs but there were Muslims and Croats among them. And there was no difference in our treatment of them, although this was an enormous financial burden for us because we were under sanctions and isolated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember November 1994 and the meeting with the Contact Group in Karadjordjevo? That is to say the full composition of the Contact Group was there visiting us.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that. They were experts, I believe, at the level of the political directors of the Member States of the Contact Group, and they reviewed the plan of the Contact Group. And the leadership of Republika Srpska was the problem, because they refused to accept the plan despite assurances that it was a good idea and smaller amendments to the plan. But the group expressed its thanks to you for the efforts you had invested to bring it to a successful close. And you asked them to do what they could for their part and to offer assurances to Republika Srpska, particularly with respect to a future confederation between the future entity and Serbia, just like the assurances that were given that the Croatia entity in Bosnia would have the right to confederation with Croatia. That was not a clear point. So that was the general gist of those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you took an active part in all these events, and I'm now going to ask you to take a look at tab 9. Let me just find your text, a short quotation, a short quotation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Mr. Robinson, that you have found tab 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not translated -- the translation is here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have the translation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before -- before we embark on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- the Chamber is, I know, considering the basis of admissibility of exhibits in respect of a previous witness. I haven't had a chance, of course, to consider this in English. I understand that this is a collection of items provided by various individuals. It may be that we're only going to be taken to something that this particular has written. The basis of admissibility ought to be explored, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this document in English, on the first page, has the name of the -- of the witness. Is this an article by him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Mr. Robinson. And to save time, I'm not going to go through the entire text. I'd like to save time, and all I'm going to ask the witness is what the reason was for him to write what I'm going to quote from his text. It's at the very end of the text. Might the text be placed on the ELMO, please? Thank you. The English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, this is from your text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us find out when it was written. When was this written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2001. As a contribution to a book devoted to the Nacertanije by Ilija Garasanin. Many authors wrote texts to accompany that work, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this a work of expertise? If so, what expertise? Is there some other basis for admissibility, because at the moment I can't see why in principle a witness should be allowed to read out something that he's written on a topic unless it has expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why not? I can't understand the basis for that objection, Mr. Nice. Let us hear what use will be made of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen it in English, and it appears to be a historical analysis of some kind. Is this man an historian? I'm doing my best to cope with a very large amount of material provided, as in this case, frequently without translation, without any statement indicating the relevance of the material, and I'm expected to, and I hope to, deal with matters in cross-examination swiftly. But the more that the gates are opened broadly to evidence of this kind, the greater it's going to be -- the harder it's going to be for me to meet those objectives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is for the Chamber to determine the weight of evidence, but he hasn't come as an expert. I don't see the point of your objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's important, Mr. Nice, that we tackle the issue you're raising to see if in fact there is an issue, because behind the objection is a complaint that you're not being given adequate notice of what's being presented. Now, all that's intended here, apparently, is a brief quotation from this document which is a statement by the witness which presumably he could be asked to make without the document in front of him, for that matter. This is a tactic similar to one that you've adopted a number of times so far and which we are considering the significance of at this moment. And it's really impossible for me to identify a basis for opposing this course of action at this moment. It may be there's no weight to be given to what's said at the end of the day, but I myself can't see a basis for objecting to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I said at the beginning I was interested to know the basis of admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has it not got to be a basis for inadmissibility that we have to seek out if there is an objection taken to evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where I have no notice of what's coming, I have to be careful. That's my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, your caution is noted, Mr. Nice. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please, for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph, you say, "With the burgeoning of the -- the demonisation of the peoples of individual nations was introduced most often as --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic start again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreter is asking you to start again, because she wasn't able to grasp it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The interpreter has found it. Yes, they do. The interpreters have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's the last page, the second half of the last paragraph, and I shall repeat: "As sense of invulnerability grew in the victor in the Cold War, the practice whereby a people in a country would be demonised was introduced, most often as a precursor to unlawful armed actions launched against them. There have been several such cases, but nowhere has the demonisation reached such total scale as in the case of Serbia and the Serbian people. A new and dangerous form of racism has appeared, no less than the kind that was manifest in colonial times. The UN should not hesitate any longer to expand its list of prohibited acts by including the prohibition of the demonisation of a country or a people. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has an absolutely legitimate and justified reason and full moral basis to launch such an initiative as soon as possible and to mobilise other countries to give their support in this effort." So this, then, is what you yourself wrote, Mr. Jovanovic. What did you have in mind in writing this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have no objection to that question, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I rather thought that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, it's the timing that matters here. I find it very difficult to adjudicate on the objection to something in the abstract on the sort of basis you tried to formulate, but I wonder, I just want to be sure that you have no objection to that question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I deal with things in order, please. It will take me a minute or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, why don't we ask the accused what is the relevance to the indictment of the so-called demonisation of the Serbian people? Deal with it as a question of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to deal with His Honour Judge Bonomy's concern, I opened this very cautiously at line, whatever it is, 28 or something. I said, "Is this a work of expertise? If so, what expertise? Is there some other basis for admissibility, because at the moment I can't see why in principle a witness should be allowed to read out something he's written on a topic unless it has expertise." There are exceptions to that, of course, if the article has been written in the course of the conflict itself and is some way a contemporaneous document, but my observation was, as I said later, cautious, and I simply wanted to know the basis of admissibility. Reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I cut through that then, Mr. Nice. Politicians or diplomats who write their memoirs of events that have occurred seem to have material which from time to time you've relied on, and indeed the accused is relying on. Now, is that not the category we've got here as a broad category? And the real question is whether the material relates to an issue that's relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly diplomats who use their books as aid memoirs and diary records and so on, that's a different category. What I was looking at was the passage to which we were referred which gave rise to my concern and cautious opening of this debate. What I now see as read out as the last ten lines would appear to be a summary and opinion. I don't understand, A, its relevance, particularly to these matters at all; B, if it's based on expertise, it hasn't come as part of an expert report and the expertise is not identified. So, Your Honour, it is certainly my submission, since you invite me to make it, that this material can be of no value to the Chamber. In light of my earlier observations which had taken quite a lot of time, and I'm always aware that if I sometimes take time to try and save time it has the contrary effect and that's why I'm very restrained in the number of objections that I make. I wasn't going to object, I was going to wait and see what the answer was and deal with it in cross-examination, but since you asked me do I object, yes, I do object. It doesn't seem to me he can take it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just so my position on this is clear, I just do not understand the concept that is being described in this piece and, therefore, the question is, as far as I can see, not aimed at anything that's relevant in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, explain the relevance of the import of these ten lines, which is the demonisation of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance, Mr. Robinson, and gentlemen, lies in the fact that this entire indictment for the most part is an expression and consequence of the demonisation of the Serb people, just as the aggression against Yugoslavia is a consequence of what was done in order to justify crimes against the Serb people. So if there is anything that is relevant and related to what you call the indictment, that is the phenomenon of the demonisation of the Serbs and the Serb people. I want to ask Mr. Jovanovic, who was a diplomat and foreign minister for many years, he formulated a proposal that the United Nations should ban all such activities, explaining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm grateful to Ms. Higgins who has put this into a context. Rather quite emotive language is used in the passage, but it comes down to the issue of one of bias, and this witness having been a foreign minister, a diplomat, and involved in international circles may well have had experiences and the opportunity to judge, as international events were faced by the FRY and before that the SFRY, as well as Serbia, and come to certain conclusions based upon his own personal experience, and it may well be that is what is at issue here in this particular passage and the reason why the evidence is being adduced in this manner, because there are issues here as to why steps were taken by NATO and the UN against Serbia, against the FRY, why Resolutions were passed more condemnatory of them than others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But he seems to be saying that the motive for the indictment is the demonisation of the Serb people, and is the motive for the indictment an issue here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The passage doesn't deal with the indictment, and that's what we have been considering. It may be that the accused has expressed his reason, having been asked to give it in that particular way, but of more importance is actually the witness's own evidence on the issue, and it may be that he's expressed it this particular way as being the pinnacle of the bias against him. But as I see it and in my submission, there are wider issues here which this witness is probably more able to be -- more able to deal with than an issue such as the indictment. I mean, that's plainly not his province to comment on the indictment, but on other issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not the first time that this issue of demonisation has occurred and the accused has presented it as a part of his case. He's seeking to say that this explains why certain actions were taken against his country. And since it is a part of his case, we will allow it. This is a majority decision, I should say. So we will allow it, but we want to have it controlled, Mr. Milosevic. I don't want any exploration of non-forensic issues. I just want a very brief explanation from the witness as to what was said in this passage, just a very brief explanation. Well, we are now at the time, but I think let us have the explanation and then we'll break. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness answers, I wish to intervene in relation to what Mr. Kay said a few moments ago. Mr. Kay said verbatim that the explanation was why NATO and the UN took measures against Yugoslavia. I think that that is quite wrong. NATO carried out an aggression against Yugoslavia in contravention of the UN Charter, without approval of the United Nations, so no one can say "NATO and the UN." That is quite in contravention of the entire system of the UN. And linking NATO action and the UN is quite inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead and answer the question, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This article and its end is a consequence of my conclusion that over a long period of time not only Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia but the people as such were exposed to terrible insults, and they were portrayed in the worst light possible. Practically there were no bounds in this anathema against the Serb people by prominent political personalities. Serbs were mentioned as a -- referred to as a subspecies, as people who had criminality in their nature, that this was an endemic thing. Also, they were referred to as a people who should be put into a cage so that not even a bird could fly out. During the war, during the aggression against Yugoslavia, the top politicians of NATO countries danced ballet with figures. They were saying that 500.000 Albanians, 10.000 Albanians, 100.000 Albanians disappeared. This was all aimed at creating this aura of the unacceptability of the Serb people. The point was in writing this to say to the UN that in spite of all this hatred and xenophobia and everything else, that demonisation should be included in such phenomena so that at least in the future other people would be protected from the kind of terrible treatment that the Serb people were subjected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. We will now take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, please open tab 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, do you want to have this exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it would be tab 9 exhibited. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 15 is a brief excerpt from a book, The New Totalitarian Society and The Destruction of Yugoslavia, by Emil Vlajki. Could you please open this. I'm just going to read a very brief quotation. Look at page 103, and this is what it says here -- tab 15, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the page he says: "[In English] This is a clear case of the bad cop/good cop game: Germany wants dissolution of Yugoslavia and the US allegedly wants the Yugoslav territorial integrity. The US 'economic' policy towards Yugoslavia proclaiming it not independent any more, ordering not only the separate 'free elections' for each republic but also the necessity of the election of political parties 'suitable' to the US standards, cutting all aid, suspending duty-free treatment, provoking the economic, political and social collapse in this country, led directly to war in the Balkans. "Moreover, in January 1991, the US warned the Yugoslav army against trying to prevent the separation of Croatia; the US --" [Interpretation] and then Susan Woodward says: "[In English] ... the US '... would not accept the use of force to hold Yugoslavia together. ... The United States was in affect telling the Yugoslav army that, in addition to its abandonment of Yugoslavia on the international front, it would consider illegitimate the army's definition of its constitutional obligation to defend the borders from the state from internal threats.'" [Interpretation] So was this good cop/bad cop approach serving political goals?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm also linking this to the testimony of the witness who came from the US senate, and he said here before you and before the public that things had to be portrayed black and white; the Serbs were black and the others were white in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, was this just prejudice or bias, or was this a deliberate policy that was aimed at conflict and disintegration of the country?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just one illustration, but there are other illustrations, too, that show that the policy of the United States of America towards the former Yugoslavia was rather hypocritical. There was a secret CIA report that they released in November 1990 that Yugoslavia would disappear within 18 months' time and that this would end in bloodshed. Then towards the end of 1990, they imposed limitations on credit and other forms of finance for the federal government for a six-month period. Then they passed a decision towards the end of 1991 to delete the name of Yugoslavia from the Most Favoured Nation list. And they also passed a few other decisions on the basis of Congress resolutions. Mr. Baker was in Yugoslavia sometime in the first half of 1990 or 1991 - I can't remember exactly just now - he had a position which was one of equidistance at first glance but it was actually in favour of Croatia and Slovenia that had intended to secede. He said that if these two republics seceded, they would not be recognised by us. That's what he said. And the federal organs cannot use force to keep them in Yugoslavia. So basically this position was in favour of secession because he guaranteed that they would not be prevented from leaving unilaterally and by force. So the US changed its -- so when people say that the US changed its position towards Yugoslavia only when the Bosnian crisis emerged, it's not true, because basically they coordinated their position with Germany and some other countries that were working to the detriment of Yugoslavia. May I also recall one more thing: That the last US ambassador to Belgrade, Mr. Zimmerman, as soon as he arrived, I think it was in 1987 or 1988, he said to all his interlocutors at federal and republican level that Yugoslavia no longer has the importance that it had before in the United States, that his country had lost strategic interest in Yugoslavia, because at that time it was quite clear that there would be no Eastern bloc any longer so it was no longer needed as a buffer state between the East and West blocs. And it really no reason to exist any longer, even more so because it was chairman of the nonaligned movement and because it had a long tradition of independence and fighting for its freedom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that and in respect of the behaviour of the military, please look at tab 13.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't interrupt at the time in view of the time consumed by my last observations, but I am not sure of the basis of admissibility of this document, but I see that the opening passage identifies the writer in terms that would suggest that the writer is an academic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we don't know whether it is being sought to be admitted. No. Mr. Kay didn't seek it. He was just reminding us. Mr. Milosevic, are you seeking the admission of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely on the basis of the fact that this clearly shows a deliberate attitude of discrimination towards the Serb side in Yugoslavia and a position that shows that it was in favour of breaking up Yugoslavia, not preserving its territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness has given his own evidence on this matter, and there is no need for its admission. We will not admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that case, please take a look at tab 13.1. This is the book by Russian historian Jelena Guskova, The History of the Yugoslav Crisis from 1990 to 2000, where on page 244 it says as follows. I'm just going to quote a small passage: "In the spring of 2001 [as interpreted], the Yugoslav People's Army was still present in all republics. Its national composition was still multinational. There were still a lot of Croats, Slovenes and Macedonians in its leadership. It was led by Veljko Kadijevic, half Croat, who considered himself a Yugoslav. His deputies were a Slovene, Admiral Stane Brovet, and a Croat Josip Greguric. Heading the aviation were Croats Antun Tus and later Zvonimir Jurjevic, commander of central military district --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In the spring of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is -- yes, tab 13.1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 244.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, this is in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have 244. We have pages 3, page 4, 5, and 6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that you just have the translation, which has been previously marked. Unfortunately, I don't have that bit translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no translation of what you were just reading, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The passage which begins, "In the spring of 1991, the Yugoslav People's Army was still present in all republics."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's in 13.2. You may find it's in 13.2 at page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 13.2 is the second volume of a different book. Yes. You have it on page 4 of the translation. You're right. That's right. "In the spring of 1991 ..." The last passage on that page, the last translated passage. That's what I just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Jovanovic, the Yugoslav People's Army was present in the entire territory of Yugoslavia. That is clear. And for how many decades prior to that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least four to five decades if we do not take into account the period of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia when a joint army also existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this bit that's translated, at the very beginning of the translation, which can be found on page 202 -- no, 212 of this book of Jelena Guskova --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, you have the translation, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the beginning of this page 4, which has a sub-heading "War."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This passage reads as follows: "However, Croatia had a different goal, which was in the end achieved after all: An independent Croatia without Serbs." So that was a goal, to have independent Croatian without Serbs. "Tudjman spoke about that on the 24th of May, 1991, in Ban Jelacic Square." I think that this date is wrong, 1991. This must be a misprint. This is a speech that we had played before in the videotape. "'A war could have been avoided but Croatia did not want that. We assessed that the independence of Croatia could be won only through war. Therefore we led a policy of negotiation while creating our own armed units by ourselves. Had we not done that, we would not have achieved the targeted goal. That means, war could have been avoided, but we would not have achieved our goal and that is the creation of our independent state.'" Jelena Guskova writes here: "An independent Croatia without Serbs." Is this in sync with what you knew about the intentions, the goals, and the achievement of those goals by means of war? So the first goal was an independent Croatia and the second one without Serbs.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said yesterday that these were two parallel strategic goals of Croatian leadership under President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was a leading question, but I rather give up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Reformulate the question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, what were the goals of Croatian policy?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goals of Croatian policy, both analysing what was quoted here and also other indicators, were to achieve by violent means a secession of Croatia from Yugoslavia. That meant causing a war because that was the only mechanism by which secession could be implemented. They were counting on foreign assistance in that endeavour. The other goal was to use intimidation, pressure, and various other means in order to force Serbs to leave Croatia, if possible immediately. And when that wasn't possible, the entire project was completed through the Operation Storm when a large number of Serbs had to leave Krajina.
