And as I said yesterday, Tudjman at a gathering expressed joy at the fact that from now on, Serbs would not constitute more than 3 to 5 per cent of the total population of Croatia. That was a public acknowledgement of ethnic cleansing which had been carried out with the use of the army in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the following passages that have been translated, in the original they can be found on page 215. It says as follows: "In August 1991, Tudjman admitted to the US ambassador that 'An all-out attack against the JNA and the Chetnik separatists' was beginning." Who were Chetnik separatists?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All Serbs who refused to accept to live under Tudjman's rule in the way that it was implemented in a very intolerant manner were considered Chetnik separatists, especially those who had to resort to arms in order to protect their lives and lives of their families and their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will continue the quotation. "When Ambassador Zimmerman proposed to Tudjman that he consider the other option, that is, giving the Serbs autonomy and thereby also abandoning war intentions, Tudjman refused to even discuss the matter."

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the beginning of the war in Croatia and Tudjman was over confident. He did not want to make any concessions to the Serbs living in Croatia. As we have heard, first he got rid of the Serbs from the constitution as a constituent nation and then he did everything that he was able to do in order to reduce the numbers of that minority and to reduce it to the percentage that Croatia could tolerate as Serb presence in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the following passage, we can see: "In late 1991, according to Tudjman's words, the Croatian armed forces numbered around 200.000 men, 350 tanks, 400 artillery pieces, 30 crop duster planes remodelled for combat operations. (85) According to other sources, the total number of Croatian armed formations reached 110.000 men, or 2.3 per cent of the population of Croatia. The largest part of the armed forces consisted of the ZNG, National Guards Corps units (about 70.000), MUP forces (around 30.000), Territorial Defence units, and finally, paramilitary formations. Also available were the armed formations of individual political parties, such as the ruling HDZ and the Croatian Party of Rights, which in 1991 began actively with ethnic cleansing in Slavonia, organised incidents and provocations and carried out the dirty work which the official structures did not want to get directly involved in." Do you know of any of these events or are you familiar with this based on the events that you know about?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unfolding of these events was very painful for Serbs living there. Already hundred thousand of Serbs had already left Croatia and fled to Serbia or some other countries, and not only from the areas which were exposed to the attack of these units but even towns where there were no conflicts. There were -- therefore, I don't know whether these figures about the Croatian formations are correct or not. Maybe they inflated this in order to impress the JNA. However, the fact is that a general mobilisation was carried out in contravention of the provisions whereby the only forces in Yugoslavia that were legal were the JNA, the police, and the Territorial Defence. So that was another violation committed by Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 211 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm having trouble finding the translation, if I've got it. I'm not sure that I have. I'm having trouble finding the original pages. I don't know if the protocols of the court require the accused to be satisfied that I can also find my way around the papers, especially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we do. Mr. Milosevic, I've already said that you must ensure that we have the pages before us before you proceed. It also goes for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I also owe it to the Court to check at this stage in any event on what's happening, because what's happening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I make two observations before you say anything, and these are directed to Mr. Milosevic. I find these questions and answers quite unhelpful. It's a clear example of leading questions to read someone else's words to a witness and then ask him if he knows anything about it. And the second comment I have to make is that with this witness, who was personally involved in matters, it seems such a waste of time to go through this exercise, especially when he's just indicated he can't actually confirm some of the material that's been put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. I have nothing else to say on the question of admissibility except I have now found the translated pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're not being helped very much by these questions, and you should move on to something else, something of which the witness has more specific and direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this is precisely what this witness gave evidence about based on his direct knowledge. Here, in a book written by an historian, we can see that his words are confirmed. This is not something that somebody else said. No. These are words of Tudjman and Izetbegovic. I assumed that Mr. Nice had the translation, because Mr. Bonomy said that he did. So if Mr. Bonomy has the translation, then Mr. Nice must have it too. And it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one comment for the interpreter. At the end of the last intervention, I said it seems such a waste of time to go through this exercise especially when the witness can't - cannot - actually confirm some of the material that's been put.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness can confirm what is being read out, because this is something that he knows as well, and I asked him about what he knew. So please take a look at the last translated excerpt, page 311. Facts are stated here, and I think that the witness has already mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think we have that pagination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 5 of the translation. There's just one single passage on page 5, in that tab, at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Does the Prosecutor have that? Yes, he does. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is a book written by an historian, and the facts are stated here. It says: "In February 1991, the SDA and the Croatian Democratic Union of BH submitted to the parliament a 'Declaration on the Sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina.' Izetbegovic stated at the time: 'For the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would sacrifice peace. For peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would not sacrifice its sovereignty.'" Mr. Jovanovic, we have Tudjman's statement given at a rally where he said there would have been no war had Croatia not wanted one, and then we have Tudjman's statement in the parliament saying that for sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, he would sacrifice peace. So what do you know about the intentions to wage war in the former Yugoslavia, both in respect of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of these leaders, Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic, were aware that they could not accomplish their goal of violent break-away with Yugoslavia without a war. So they counted on this war and accepted it consciously. I would like to add to the statement of Izetbegovic presented here another one that he uttered in discussion with Lord Carrington, where he said that he knew that in order to achieve independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it will be necessary to -- to -- to go to war, to a civil war. We have already mentioned the Belgrade initiative here, and together with Momir Bulatovic, you invited the then leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina to come to Belgrade and to discuss the current situation. You received only a response from the then-speaker of the parliament, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, whereas Mr. Izetbegovic did not reply at all. Therefore, he did not want to find a peaceful solution to the existing situation through consensus with other leaders, which meant that he had opted for the other possibility, which led to war. That means that the intention for causing war in Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot be attributed to Serbia and Montenegro at all but, rather, to those who planned to carry out a violent break-away with the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you explain in rather precise terms during your testimony here what the positions of various Western politicians were. I mentioned the positions held by politicians on both sides of the Atlantic. Now, please take a look at tab 13.2. This is the second volume of the history written by Jelena Guskova. Page 24.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you have the translation. Let me just make sure that you do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Read out the first passage and let's check whether it's in 13.1 or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very briefly. I was confused by the name of the publisher. Just a second. Yes, you have the translation. I hope all of you have it. "The Secretary-General of the UN, Perez de Cuellar, in December, 1991..." In the English translation it starts "In December 1991..." In December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, page 4 of 13.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "... wrote to Hans Van den Broek, the president of the European Community Council of Ministers, as well as to German Foreign Minister Hans-Detrich Genscher, that selective recognition of the Yugoslav republics could 'contribute to a spread of the present conflict and the intensification of the explosive situation.'" With respect to recognition, an active role was taken by the Vatican. The Vatican also took an active role in connection with the recognition of Croatia and Slovenia, and you mentioned that yesterday, Mr. Jovanovic. "On 26 November 1991, Cardinal Sodano invited the ambassadors of the United States of America, France, Great Britain, Belgium, Italy, Germany and Austria, accredited in the Holy See, and informed them of the Vatican's stand, insisting that their countries recognise Slovenia and Croatia in the same month. Describing that meeting, US Ambassador Melady said he was convinced that there had been prior consent between the Vatican, Germany, Austria and Italy, because the ambassadors of those countries enthusiastically supported the Vatican's proposal." Then he goes on to say: "In Lord Carrington's opinion, Europe made two mistakes. 'I think it would have been better,' he noted in the fall of 1992, 'had Europe accepted the break-up of Yugoslavia earlier. According to the plan that I proposed in the summer of 1991, six republics committed, on the one hand, to have more or less close mutual relations, while on the other, the centre would survive. Some of them claimed they were ready for such an alliance. But the European Twelve did not listen to me, because they were afraid that such a plan would serve as a precedent for the break-up of the Russian Federation. Europe's second mistake was to recognise Croatia and Slovenia. The goal of convening the European conference, which I chaired, was to postpone the recognition of the independence of these two republics until global consent of the six Yugoslav republics was achieved. Their recognition undermined the basis of our work, which was reduced to simple bilateral negotiations, all the more so as it was later considered necessary to also ask Bosnia about its desire for independence. Of course, Alija Izetbegovic could only respond in the affirmative. I warned the leaders of the European Community that such a scenario, unacceptable for the Serbs in Bosnia, would lead to civil war. That was a tragic mistake.'" And furthermore he says: "US Secretary of State Warren Christopher wrote in June 1993 that responsibility lay in particular with the Germans, because they managed to convince their partners in the European Community to recognise Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Using an illogical approach, Germany claimed that non-recognition of --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have read such a long passage. What meaningful question can you now ask of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the meaningful question is this: Is what is being quoted about Carrington's stand, Perez de Cuellar's views, the Vatican's views, Sodano and the ambassadors of the countries I've quoted, does it coincide with your knowledge of what happened at the time? Is this in collision with what you know? Is something incorrect here, or is it correct? Is what they say here true? And you spoke about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention something about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... formulation of the question reveals the need to get round of the problem of its being leading in nature. At the moment we're not interested in the accuracy or otherwise of what the author says. It may happen when the author comes to give evidence, if she does or he does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's now going to testify as to facts within his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case then it's just because it's entirely leading that the question is objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The point being made, Mr. Milosevic, is that when you read out a passage like this and then ask the witness whether his experience coincides with that, you have actually given him the answer from the passage. And so it is -- it is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm not going to ask him. Well, Mr. Jovanovic is an adult, an experienced man. He's a politician. I don't assume he needs me to explain to him what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I read out these passages -- well, I'm asking you now, Mr. Jovanovic, whether what I read out, what it says there is correct or incorrect.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, because it was repeated several times on several occasions in different books and newspapers, and I should like to add to that this: Mr. De Michelis, for example, a high-ranking official of the European Community, before the conference stopped work during the summer of 1991, issued warnings of the danger of premature recognition of Slovenia and Croatia by Germany and that the Security Council in three of its Resolutions at that time issued warnings of the danger of premature recognition and appealed to all states, especially members of the European Community, to refrain from any act or step which could lead to an escalation of tensions and make the successful conclusion of the conference difficult. After that, more or less all the statesmen of repute and renown in the East and in the West presented their critical views on the issue, and I should like to mention in particular Kissinger, Baker, and the rest. Mr. Baker, for example, expressly stated that Germany's actions in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the European Community with respect to the premature recognition of these two republics and later Bosnia-Herzegovina was a direct cause of war, and he said it was the trigger of the war. And there were similar statements, and with hindsight, of course, they spoke critically about this wrong step, wrong move that was made in December and January, December 1991 and January 1992 when the three republics were recognised through this speedy accelerated process and thereby a long and bloody war was unleashed, especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, Lord Carrington said there were two mistakes. You've dealt with one of them, which was premature recognition. The other one, he says, was that Europe should have accepted the break-up of Yugoslavia earlier than it did. Do you accept that also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That break-up was not done earlier for it to have been accepted. It was started immediately prior to the conference, and at the conference the process was accelerated, because two documents were presented to the conference. One was an arrangement for a general solution, and the second was a contract for a general solution in which Yugoslavia was not mentioned any more, just its federal units with their interest in breaking away or, rather, others remaining within Yugoslavia. So I think that Lord Carrington's remark was and criticism of the European Community was that it made it impossible for the political process led by the Conference on Yugoslavia to be rounded off and completed and then those who wished to secede be recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, it says the following -- De Michelis's explanation, he says: "We were facing Maastricht. Nobody could allow a split in the alliance --" and he is referring to the European Community of the day -- "but it was more than clear to me with that decision, we spurred the fire in Bosnia, and maybe also in Kosovo" wrote Gianni De Michelis, former Italian Foreign Minister.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is a question. What was Italy's position at the time, or De Michelis's position specifically with regard to the events in Yugoslavia? He came to visit. I assume you met him on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet him, but Italy, according to Mitterand's words, was handicapped by the position taken by the Vatican, which tied its hands. And so for a long time in a way it was a silent participant in this process until De Michelis and Genscher met in Venice, and that was in the autumn of 1991 - I forget the exact date - when they expressed their support to the intentions of Slovenia and Croatia to secede. And as far as this hindsight on the part of De Michelis is concerned, he could have done that earlier. He could have prevented it all earlier. As far as Maastricht is concerned, let me point one thing out: Maastricht was an agreement by others at the detriment of Yugoslavia. To calm down Germany and Austria, it was decided to abolish Yugoslavia and to recognise the two republics that wished to secede. So that was also stated in Mr. Vedrine's book. And he said that Great Britain had managed to convince France to accept the German demand in exchange for the fact that Germany had agreed to the conditions of the monetary union and because some political concepts were rejected with respect to the integration into the European Union. That is to say, Germany gave up on some of its other conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Very well. Now, on page 28, and now we're going through what you mentioned partially yesterday, Guskova has a brief quotation here. It is also translated, and it is this: "Many politicians later understood the negative consequences of the hasty recognition of the former Yugoslav republics. Cyrus Vance said how the Hague Agreement should have been adhered to, which did not permit recognition of the former Yugoslav republics until a political solution acceptable for all was found. James Baker was even more downright: 'Slovenia and Croatia are responsible for the civil war in the former Yugoslavia. Their forcible secession, contrary to the acts of the Helsinki agreement, pushed Yugoslavia directly into settling accounts by military means. It is a fact that Slovenia and Croatia proclaimed their independence unilaterally in spite of our warnings, that they used force in order to capture border posts, which provoked civil war.' In Henry Kissinger's opinion, "Western democrats should have thought twice before they recognised a Balkan state whose borders in the ethnic, linguistic and historical sense did not coincide with the traditional concept of a nation and a state. How could Western politicians even imagine that the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims - whose mutual hatred led to the break-up of Yugoslavia - could co-exist and live together in an even smaller Bosnian state?'" Now, Mr. Jovanovic, do you have an example of any serious world politician who did not indicate the fatal mistakes that were made by the international community in the Yugoslav crisis? Can you quote me a single example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm not allowing that. It's not the international community that is on trial. So I won't allow that question. But I wanted to ask you, it is part of your case, isn't it, that the secession of Slovenia and Croatia and the premature -- their premature recognition was what led to the conflict and not any act on your part. Is that part of your -- is that your case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite obviously there was no act on Serbia's part which could have caused the conflict and war. If you take a look at the chronology of events and everything that happened, you can see that for yourselves. You have access to all the exhibits, evidence, and proof. You have proof how fast Serbia -- what Serbia did to avoid war, and what it did to establish peace in areas where war did break out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the passage you just quoted from James Baker, he said: "Their forcible secession, contrary to the acts of the Helsinki agreement, pushed Yugoslavia directly into settling accounts by military means." So he's there saying that as a result of their secession, Yugoslavia was obliged to settle accounts by military means. And do you accept that? That's the passage you cited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you interpreted that in the proper manner. They didn't interpret Baker properly. When Baker says "Yugoslavia" he doesn't mean the federal authorities, he means the country as a whole, within its borders within which armed conflicts had begun, because that happened as a result of that. And Baker knew full well how the military conflicts began. The Yugoslav People's Army certainly didn't begin them. So he refers to Yugoslavia, not the federal authorities or federal institutions but the country Yugoslavia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a nice distinction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's a very vital difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's -- you seem to take it for granted everything written in this history book is true. They may be, but they are not legally so unless the Prosecution agrees to it. So you have to establish, first of all, whether it is true that such people said such things to the knowledge of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the politicians? Is that what you're referring to? Well, what these politicians said was public. They were public statements, and as far as I remember, I quoted some of those politicians, referring to the source. But you can establish that -- we can establish that once again if need be. And I'm not taking things for granted. It's impossible that everything is true and correct in a book written by an author, but I assume that the author did his best or her best to present the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Take the advantage of the presence of this witness. Establish those facts with the assistance of this witness, as far as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, what, out of all these observations, do you think might be incorrect with respect to the causes of the conflict on the territory of Yugoslavia? We always speak about conflicts, armed conflicts on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. That's what we're talking about, are we not?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think these quotations have been taken in their correct form, taken over in their correct form because they are to be found in the books of other authors. For example, in Hubert Vedrine's Les mondes de Francois Mitterrand, there are a lot of quotations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have that book. It is an exhibit. We'll go through it, not all the quotations, we won't have time for that, but we shall go into some of them.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we have Mr. Gumper [phoen], who was a high-ranking official in the National Security Council of President Bush, for example, Bush and Clinton. And he was quoted -- quotes from his speech at the Council of Foreign Relations in New York, and he said that this was a trigger. This triggered the war in Yugoslavia, the recognition. And we have the books of other authors, French author Bauzin [phoen] and Daniel Danage [phoen], Jean Gonan [phoen], for example, which -- where you will find quotes from other statesmen including the ones here. So it's not the quotations that can be challenged. We can ask ourselves whether the people who saw the situation as being such, whether the situation was actually like that, but you can't question the quotes because it is a fact that that is what they said and they said that in public forums. For example, the American Congress in 1995. So he did have some responsibility before Congress in presenting observations of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, who said what in the American Congress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] James Baker said that in the US Congress sometime in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The quotation that's on the page that we're reading was said in the US Congress, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. That's the way it was put. Along with other sentences, but of course this excerpt is characteristic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You accept that that quotation, if it's accurate, means that America wasn't behind Slovenia and Croatia proclaiming their independence, that America was against it? That's what the statement says. And it seems to be Mr. Milosevic's case that America was one of the conspirators encouraging that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said -- if you are putting the question to me, I beg your pardon. I hope I can answer it now. I already said that the real American policy was the one that followed from concrete action; the statement made by Ambassador Zimmerman that Yugoslavia lost its strategic importance for America, and then also intentionally releasing the secret CIA report that Yugoslavia would disappear within 18 months' time, and in blood at that. Then also denying the federal government assistance for six months but also not denying any assistance to the federal republics -- federal units. Then also deleting Yugoslavia from the list of Most Favoured Nations. That was done in December 1991. There is also a decision that had to do with the so-called repressive policies in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, Mr. Jovanovic. I remember your evidence about these various matters, but basically are you saying Mr. Baker was being hypocritical, saying one thing and doing something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I just wish to recall the facts, what was happening in 1990 and 1991, including the visit paid by Mr. Baker to all the Yugoslav republics and to the federal government sometime in the first half the 1991 where he set up this well-known equidistance. In my opinion, it was not real equidistance, it was actually a signal to the federal units that without fear from any use of force or from the federal government, they could secede from Yugoslavia. His statement in 1995 is probably due to the need to shift at least part of the blame for the violent, bloody break-up of Yugoslavia elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll have to shorten this because I'm not going to be able to quote everything, especially because there's no need for me to quote Clinton here saying that I played a key role in Dayton. That is a generally known fact, and I hope that you are sufficiently aware of it, too, that I played that kind of role in the attainment of peace. However, there will be opportunities, and I hope that we will have the opportunity of hearing and seeing Jelena Guskova, who has been dealing with the Yugoslav crisis for many, many years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you mentioned the French foreign minister, Hubert Vedrine.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to draw your attention to tab 10, Les mondes de Francois Mitterrand by Hubert Vedrine, a close co-worker of President Mitterrand's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does the Chamber want to decide about tab 13 in accordance with its practice? It would seem to me it should not be admitted. The author, in any event, is coming to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tabs 13.2 and 13.1 have generated a great deal of discussion as well as inquiry from the Bench. In my submission, they should be exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Consistent with past practice, the witness has given evidence himself, so we will not admit that tab.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand this right, Mr. Robinson. Why are you refusing these quotations on the basis of which I put so many questions to Mr. Jovanovic and he testified about that? Why can that not be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because we are not helped by it. I mean, the witness has given the evidence himself, so it doesn't really add anything that is useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can call Jelena Guskova to exhibit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If that applies to all books, then no books should be admitted into evidence. You can always say the author of the book has to be called. You have introduced many quotations from many books into evidence, admitted them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have ruled on that, Mr. Milosevic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, please, Vedrine's book. I'm going to ask you to read these quotations, since you speak French, and a few quotations have been marked here, the ones that I want you to read out. First on page 618, Maastricht is the sub-heading, and after the second paragraph it says: "[No interpretation]". Could you please read it out for us.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read it in French or in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please read it in French because the book is written in French. You don't have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But do I have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you please read out the original. The book is written in French. The author is French, and he wrote the book in French.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "After Maastricht, the talks among the 12 made rapid progress. On the 14th, Javier Perez de Cuellar regretted the move to recognise the former Yugoslav republics in a premature, selective and uncoordinated manner." That's the first quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The author is Hubert Vedrine, the French foreign minister, and he's talking about Mitterrand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that this can be taken as authentic, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To what end? It just seems to me that you're repeating. We have been over this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Robinson, but you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the premature recognition of these countries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Robinson, you always point out that you seek additional evidence to support some assertion. You now believe that all of this is proven and that there is no need for me to give any additional evidence. I'll only be too glad to stop at this point, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you have only a few more quotations from the book -- from the book marked here about the years of Francois Mitterrand that Vedrine wrote. Could you please be so kind as to read the next paragraph that is marked here, and it says, "That seemed fair." It's not readily visible.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. "This seemed fair, but calling for a referendum even to provide guarantees was, nevertheless, dangerous. Even under Tito, the assent of the three communities of Bosnia-Herzegovina (Muslims, Serbs, and Croats) appeared so essential to the proper functioning of the republic that it was required, as I mentioned, for almost all decisions. A majority of votes was not sufficient since, in terms of numbers, two of the three Bosnian communities could easily impose on the third a decision Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that would be unacceptable to it. Therefore, a referendum in the specific case of Bosnia only appeared to be a good idea, an apparently democratic move which was actually explosive. Unless it were to crown successful negotiations, which would not be the case, quite the contrary, Robert Badinter commented that the members of the commission primarily had in mind --" there is no sequel to this. That's where it ends. Let me just see where this is. It's the end of the passage. There is no end to this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now what Badinter said is --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whoever may be interested in this can look it up.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the last passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Francois Mitterrand himself is being quoted here, the 23rd of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 23rd of February, 1993, recalling that period, Francois Mitterrand told Andreas Papandreou: 'It was all a sequence of errors: The German move, the American ignorance, the hesitation of the Italians as Italy was paralysed by the statements of the Holy See. In fact, Germany sees itself as the legitimate heir of the Austro-Hungarian Empire and has taken on Austria's old grudge against the Serbs.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can understand, this is from Hubert Vedrine's book, but he directly quoted Francois Mitterrand in this book about Mitterrand?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because he was present at the meeting with Papandreou?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a quotation. The third bit I read out is a quotation from the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you read out just now, what Mitterrand said, is that correct, since you also know about this behaviour of Germany and its activities?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this is correct. I have already referred to this, but a lot can be said about this. Throughout the Yugoslav crisis, especially at the very outset, it behaved in a highly partial manner and it boldly and openly supported one side, that is say the secession of Slovenia and Croatia. As I said yesterday, Minister Genscher, as a matter of fact, only a day or two before these two republics proclaimed their independence, he within the European Community raised the question of their independence, as he said, "that would soon be proclaimed." So he even acted in advance of the actual proclamation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, please, in relation to the nature of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, could you please quote Vedrine, what he says on page 634. That is the very beginning of the passage. That is what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The main reason lies in the nature of the conflict. In Bosnia, let me say it again, there is no invader and invaded, as was the case in Kuwait. There are three Bosnian communities which, with foreign aid, are fighting for land, valleys and mountains throughout the country, one of those communities being more aggressive than the others."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, what was the nature of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a conflict among the three communities. And a typical example of a civil war that was started for the reasons I referred to yesterday, because two communities joined up against a third one and they only took part in the referendum that was imposed. Many other assessments made by foreign statesmen also indicate the fact that this was a civil war. Not only Vedrine. Even President Clinton twice, when he was under pressure to intervene in Bosnia-Herzegovina and at the time he was not willing to do so, he said twice publicly that in Bosnia there was a civil war going on. He said that in public. And later on, he changed that when he was prepared for military intervention in Bosnia-Herzegovina through NATO. So the three sides were waging a fratricidal civil war, a religious war at times, and there was also a separate civil war that was going on between two different Muslim sides. On the secessionist side was Abdic and on the other side was the leadership of the Muslim people. So if the three sides were engaged in incessant conflict there and if one of the three sides was split up in two and was engaged in its own conflict, one cannot speak of an international conflict. It is certain that all three sides had their aiders and abettors from the outside because there is no civil war without any such external aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, one part of that quotation at the end was that one of the three communities was more aggressive than the others. Which community was Vedrine referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume he meant the Serb community, because that community was a victim of these political manipulations in relation to organising the referendum. Both constitutions of Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina guaranteed constituent status to all constituent nations in Yugoslavia, and this insolent aim at reducing them -- to reduce them to a minority brought this about. This was to be expected when Bosnia and Herzegovina was instructed to organise a referendum as a precondition for gaining independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you bringing your examination-in-chief to an end now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a number of questions outstanding, so I cannot complete immediately. If you are to ask for a break now, I wouldn't mind that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope not more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to take the break now. Mr. Nice, the discussion we were going to have, which I haven't really characterised as a hearing, we'll call on you first to address us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit status of tab 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or non-status, as I would urge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit this one. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As I indicated earlier, we're going to have a brief discussion of this motion. Mr. Sasa Obradovic is here. Would you please sit. He's the representative of the government of Serbia and Montenegro. Mr. Nice, the first issue is are we to be in private session or in open session for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would have thought, given the nature of the underlying concern of Serbia and Montenegro, it would be preferable to be in private session for the time being, with the liberty -- not liberty, with the facility to open up the hearings at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do that. We'll start in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 1 --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday the 16th day of February, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
